## At a glance

**Guiding question:** To which new case should the claim refer?\
**For:** doctoral researchers in preclinical imaging, clinical research teams planning a validation, reviewers of
prediction and imaging studies · **Prerequisites:** units of analysis and denominators (@sec-b03), training and test
data with a baseline (@sec-b05), spectra and the hyperspectral measurement chain (@sec-b10)\
**In the course:** [W4 · What imaging, gait and tissue models measure](https://cttir.github.io/clinical-data-science-in-r-course/lessons/w4-imaging-gait-tissue.html)
(required reading), also used in
[W6 · Pharmacometrics, forecasting and simulation](https://cttir.github.io/clinical-data-science-in-r-course/lessons/w6-pharmacometrics-forecasting-simulation.html)
and [W8 · Model colloquium and decision](https://cttir.github.io/clinical-data-science-in-r-course/lessons/w8-colloquium-and-decision.html)
· **Data:** synthetic (generated in the chapter) · **Core reading time:** about 10 minutes
:::

## Case and decision {#sec-b19-case}

A doctoral researcher in a preclinical imaging group presents a slide at the lab meeting: a classifier separates two
tissue classes, A and B, in hyperspectral reflectance spectra, and the test accuracy is 100%. The data come from four
animals with three spectra each. The group leader wants to quote the result in a funding application for a first
feasibility study in patients with soft-tissue injuries. Before the sentence goes into the application, a methods
reviewer in the group asks one question: *which new case was the test about?* A further spectrum from an animal that
the model has already seen, a new animal from the same laboratory, an animal measured next year with a new camera, or
a patient? The answer decides what the group may write. If the test only measured recognition of known animals, the
application would ask patients to carry the burden of a study whose central premise was never tested.

## Core reading {#sec-b19-core}

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple" icon=false}
**Core reading** · required for W4 · about 10 minutes · ends before ‘Lab’
:::

Every test answers a question about a particular kind of new case. A model evaluated on new spectra from animals it
has already seen answers the question "does it recognise more data from these animals?". A model evaluated on animals
it has never seen answers "does it work for a new animal from the same setting?". Neither answers "does it work in
another centre, with another device, or in another species?". The skill this chapter trains is to name the intended
new case *before* choosing the split, and then to check that the split really produces such cases.

**Five levels of "new".** It helps to list the levels explicitly (@tbl-b19-levels). Each row needs its own test,
and a positive result on an upper row says nothing about the rows below it. The general idea of keeping training and
test data apart is covered in @sec-b05 and in
[Methods in R: Train-Test Splits](https://cttir.github.io/methods-in-r/sec-ch-13-ml.html#sec-chapters-13-ml-train-test-split);
here the point is which *unit* must be new.

| Intended new case | Split that produces it | Independent denominator |
|---|---|---|
| Another spectrum or image of a known animal | Image-wise: spectra of each animal on both sides | Spectra (but they are not independent) |
| A new animal, same laboratory and device | Animal-wise (group split): every animal on one side only | Animals in the test set |
| A later animal, after protocol drift | Temporal: train on earlier, test on later animals | Animals measured after the cut-off |
| Another centre, device or operator | External: develop at one site, test at another | Animals (or patients) at the new site |
| Another species, or patients | A new study in the target population | Individuals of the target species |

: Levels of "new" and the split that tests each one. The denominator is the number of independent units that the claim is about. {#tbl-b19-levels}

**A deliberately trivial example.** Four fictitious animals, T1 to T4, each contribute three spectra. The classes are
properties of animals: T1 and T3 belong to class A, T2 and T4 to class B. Instead of a real classifier we use a
didactic model that is constructed to cheat in a transparent way. It never looks at a spectrum. For an animal ID it
has seen during training, it returns the class it recorded for that animal. For any other ID it returns a fallback
class that was fixed in advance: class A. Call it the *recall model*. If a test cannot distinguish this model from a
useful one, the test is not informative about new animals.

```{r}
#| label: fig-b19-splitplan
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 3.4
#| fig-cap: "Two split plans for the same 12 synthetic spectra (n = 4 animals; classes A/B are properties of animals). Grey tiles are training data, white tiles test data; the text gives the recall model's result. Left: image-wise split, 4 of 4 test spectra right. Right: animal-wise split, 3 of 6 test spectra and 1 of 2 test animals right. Data status: synthetic."
#| fig-alt: "Two tile charts side by side. Rows are animals T1 (class A), T2 (B), T3 (A) and T4 (B); columns are spectrum 1, 2 and 3. In the left panel, titled image-wise split, spectra 1 and 2 of every animal are grey training tiles and spectrum 3 of every animal is a white test tile labelled right, giving four right out of four. In the right panel, titled animal-wise split, all spectra of T1 and T2 are grey training tiles; the three spectra of T3 are white test tiles labelled right and the three spectra of T4 are white test tiles labelled wrong, giving three right out of six spectra and one right out of two animals."
library(ggplot2)
plan_animals <- data.frame(id = c("T1", "T2", "T3", "T4"), class = c("A", "B", "A", "B"))
plan <- merge(plan_animals, data.frame(spectrum = 1:3))
plan <- rbind(
  transform(plan, design = "Image-wise split: 4/4 right",
            role = ifelse(spectrum == 3, "test", "train")),
  transform(plan, design = "Animal-wise split: 3/6 spectra, 1/2 animals right",
            role = ifelse(id %in% c("T3", "T4"), "test", "train"))
)
plan$design <- factor(plan$design, levels = unique(plan$design))
# recall model result for test tiles: known ID -> recorded class, unknown ID -> class A
known_ids <- ifelse(grepl("^Image", plan$design), TRUE, plan$id %in% c("T1", "T2"))
plan$pred <- ifelse(known_ids, plan$class, "A")
plan$label <- ifelse(plan$role == "train", "train",
                     ifelse(plan$pred == plan$class, "test:\nright", "test:\nwrong"))
plan$row <- factor(paste0(plan$id, " (", plan$class, ")"), levels = rev(c("T1 (A)", "T2 (B)", "T3 (A)", "T4 (B)")))
ggplot(plan, aes(x = factor(spectrum), y = row, fill = role)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "black", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_text(aes(label = label), size = 3.1, lineheight = 0.85) +
  facet_wrap(~ design) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(train = "grey80", test = "white"), guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Spectrum number within animal", y = "Animal (class)",
       caption = "Synthetic teaching example. Recall model: known ID returns the recorded class, unknown ID returns class A.") +
  theme_cdsr() +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank())
```

**What the two designs show.** In the image-wise split, two spectra of every animal are used for training and the
third for testing. Every test ID is known, so the recall model gets 4 of 4 right. It has measured recognition, not
classification. In the animal-wise split, T1 (A) and T2 (B) are used for training; T3 (A) and T4 (B) with three spectra
each form the test set. Both IDs are unknown, so the fallback class A is returned six times: 3 of 6 spectra are right,
and at the level of animals 1 of 2. The independent denominator is two animals, not six spectra. A result of "50%"
from two animals is compatible with almost anything; it is a statement about two individuals.

**The most important assumption.** **A test is informative about the intended new case only if the unit that is new
in the test is the unit that the claim is about, and the denominator counts those units.** For a claim about new
animals the test must contain animals the model has never seen, and accuracy must be reported per animal. In R this
is one line: `intersect(unique(train$id), unique(test$id))` must be empty for the animal-wise split. The same leak
appears under many names in the literature, from pseudoreplication to "data leakage" [@kapoor2023leakage], and
grouped or blocked cross-validation is the standard remedy for clustered data [@roberts2017crossvalidation].

**Beyond the group split.** An empty ID intersection is necessary, not sufficient. A clinical prediction model can be
*reproducible* in new patients from the same population yet fail to be *transportable* to a different but related
population [@justice1999generalizability]. External validation is therefore interpreted against the difference in
case mix between development and validation samples [@debray2015framework]. Two further shifts matter in imaging.
A change in measurement procedure (camera, illumination, calibration, operator) can alter spectra in ways that a model
learns as if it were biology; an imaging model for chest radiographs, for example, could identify the hospital system
of a radiograph almost perfectly, which can confound its predictions [@zech2018pneumonia]. And a change of
species is not a larger version of a change of centre. Whether mouse models "mimic" human inflammatory responses after
trauma and burns has been answered in opposite directions from the same gene expression data, depending on which genes
were compared [@seok2013mouse; @takao2015mouse]. The lesson for this chapter is modest: similarity between species is a
claim with its own analysis choices, and a model trained in animals makes no claim about patients until it has been
tested in patients.

**What the reviewer writes back.** "The 100% result is an image-wise test. It supports the statement that spectra
of the four known animals can be recognised. For new animals, the independent denominator is the number of test
animals; please report the animal-wise result with its denominator. A statement about patients needs a study in
patients." The finding is not worthless. It is an honest description of what was tested, and it points to the next
study, which in preclinical work also has to justify the number of animals under the 3Rs (@sec-b16).

**Question for the workshop:** Your group has spectra from six animals measured in two laboratories with two cameras.
Write down the intended new case for your claim, the split that produces it, and the denominator you would report. Which
row of @tbl-b19-levels can your data not reach at all?

## Lab {#sec-b19-lab}

The lab has three parts. First, the hand calculation from the core reading is reproduced exactly, with target values.
Second, a self-contained variant uses a nearest-neighbour model on synthetic spectra with the same animal IDs; its
results are kept in separate objects. Third, a deepening exercise treats a missing modality as a stress test.

::: {.callout-note title="R start command"}
From the root of the book repository, render the chapter:

```bash
quarto render chapters/b19-transfer-across-centres-and-species.qmd --to html
```

To run only the R code in a fresh R session, start from the `chapters/` folder:

```bash
Rscript -e 'source(knitr::purl("b19-transfer-across-centres-and-species.qmd", output = tempfile(fileext = ".R"), quiet = TRUE))'
```

The chapter writes the synthetic spectra and the fold assignment to `data/b19-spectra.csv`.
:::

### Raw values and the recall model

The input is a table with one row per spectrum. Only the ID and the class are needed for the hand calculation, because
the recall model does not use the spectrum.

```{r}
#| label: b19-raw
# one row per spectrum: animal ID, class of the animal, spectrum number
animals <- data.frame(id = c("T1", "T2", "T3", "T4"), class = c("A", "B", "A", "B"))
spectra <- merge(animals, data.frame(spectrum = 1:3))
spectra <- spectra[order(spectra$id, spectra$spectrum), ]
rownames(spectra) <- NULL
spectra

# didactic recall model: known ID -> class recorded in training; unknown ID -> fallback class "A"
fit_recall <- function(train, fallback = "A") {
  known <- unique(train[, c("id", "class")])
  function(test_id) {
    hit <- match(test_id, known$id)
    ifelse(is.na(hit), fallback, known$class[hit])
  }
}
```

### Image-wise split: recognition

```{r}
#| label: b19-imagewise
train_img <- spectra[spectra$spectrum %in% 1:2, ]   # two spectra per animal for training
test_img  <- spectra[spectra$spectrum == 3, ]       # third spectrum of every animal for testing
pred_img  <- fit_recall(train_img)(test_img$id)

hand_img_correct <- sum(pred_img == test_img$class)
hand_img_shared  <- intersect(unique(train_img$id), unique(test_img$id))
hand_img_correct; hand_img_shared

stopifnot(hand_img_correct == 4, nrow(test_img) == 4)  # 4/4 right spectra
stopifnot(length(hand_img_shared) == 4)                 # all four animals on both sides
```

### Animal-wise split: new animals

```{r}
#| label: b19-animalwise
train_ani <- spectra[spectra$id %in% c("T1", "T2"), ]   # one A and one B animal for training
test_ani  <- spectra[spectra$id %in% c("T3", "T4"), ]   # one new A and one new B animal
test_ani$pred <- fit_recall(train_ani)(test_ani$id)

hand_ani_spectra <- sum(test_ani$pred == test_ani$class)
# animal level: an animal counts as right if its spectra are classified as its class
per_animal <- aggregate(cbind(right = pred == class) ~ id, data = test_ani, FUN = all)
hand_ani_animals <- sum(per_animal$right)
hand_ani_shared  <- intersect(unique(train_ani$id), unique(test_ani$id))
per_animal; hand_ani_spectra; hand_ani_animals; hand_ani_shared

stopifnot(hand_ani_spectra == 3, nrow(test_ani) == 6)   # 3/6 right spectra
stopifnot(hand_ani_animals == 1, nrow(per_animal) == 2) # 1/2 right animals; denominator = 2 animals
stopifnot(length(hand_ani_shared) == 0)                 # empty ID intersection
```

The hand calculation gives `r hand_img_correct`/4 in the image-wise test and `r hand_ani_spectra`/6 spectra or
`r hand_ani_animals`/2 animals in the animal-wise test. These values belong to the recall model and are fixed by
construction; they do not depend on any random number.

### A split plan with zero ID overlap

A split plan is a small table that is written down before any model is fitted: one row per fold, the IDs on each
side, and the number of shared IDs. For four animals and two classes, a two-fold group split keeps one A and one B
animal on each side, and both folds together use every animal once as a test animal.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-b19-splitplan
#| tbl-cap: "Split plan for the animal-wise design (two folds, n = 4 animals). Shared IDs must be zero in every fold. Data status: synthetic."
fold_of <- c(T1 = 2, T2 = 2, T3 = 1, T4 = 1)            # test fold of each animal
split_plan <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:2, function(f) {
  test_ids  <- names(fold_of)[fold_of == f]
  train_ids <- names(fold_of)[fold_of != f]
  data.frame(fold = f,
             train_animals = paste(train_ids, collapse = ", "),
             test_animals = paste(test_ids, collapse = ", "),
             test_spectra = sum(spectra$id %in% test_ids),
             shared_ids = length(intersect(train_ids, test_ids)))
}))
stopifnot(all(split_plan$shared_ids == 0),
          setequal(unlist(strsplit(split_plan$test_animals, ", ")), animals$id))
knitr::kable(split_plan, col.names = c("Fold", "Training animals", "Test animals", "Test spectra", "Shared IDs"))
```

### Self-contained variant: a nearest-neighbour model

The next block runs on its own in a fresh R session. It generates synthetic reflectance spectra for the same IDs T1 to
T4 and classifies them with a one-nearest-neighbour model (`class::knn`, @venables2002mass; method background in
[Methods in R: k-Nearest Neighbours Classification](https://cttir.github.io/methods-in-r/sec-ch-13-ml.html#sec-chapters-13-ml-knn-classification)).
Each animal has its own level and slope of reflectance (an individual "signature"), and class B adds a weak dip in the
near infrared. **These spectra are an assumption made for teaching: the animal signature is deliberately stronger
than the class signal.** All results are stored with the prefix `knn_`, so they cannot be confused with the hand
calculation.

```{r}
#| label: b19-knn
#| warning: false
library(class)
set.seed(4419)  # own seed: this block does not depend on earlier chunks

knn_make_spectra <- function(class_effect = 0.03, ids = c("T1", "T2", "T3", "T4"),
                             classes = c("A", "B", "A", "B"), n_per_animal = 3,
                             animal_sd = 0.05, noise_sd = 0.004) {
  wl <- seq(500, 940, by = 40)                                # wavelength in nm
  base <- 0.30 + 0.30 / (1 + exp(-(wl - 690) / 25))          # common tissue curve (reflectance, 0-1)
  rows <- list()
  for (i in seq_along(ids)) {
    level <- rnorm(1, 0, animal_sd)                          # animal-specific offset
    slope <- rnorm(1, 0, animal_sd)                          # animal-specific tilt
    dip <- if (classes[i] == "B") class_effect * exp(-((wl - 800) / 70)^2) else 0
    for (s in seq_len(n_per_animal)) {
      refl <- base + level + slope * (wl - 720) / 220 - dip + rnorm(length(wl), 0, noise_sd)
      rows[[length(rows) + 1]] <- data.frame(id = ids[i], class = classes[i], spectrum = s,
                                             wavelength_nm = wl, reflectance = refl)
    }
  }
  do.call(rbind, rows)
}
knn_to_wide <- function(long) {
  w <- reshape(long, idvar = c("id", "class", "spectrum"), timevar = "wavelength_nm", direction = "wide")
  rownames(w) <- NULL
  w
}
# 1-NN prediction; optional: columns missing at test time are replaced by training means
knn_predict <- function(wide, train, test, available = NULL) {
  X <- as.matrix(wide[, grep("^reflectance", names(wide))])
  if (!is.null(available)) {
    missing_cols <- setdiff(seq_len(ncol(X)), available)
    X[test, missing_cols] <- matrix(colMeans(X[train, missing_cols, drop = FALSE]),
                                    sum(test), length(missing_cols), byrow = TRUE)
  }
  as.character(knn(X[train, , drop = FALSE], X[test, , drop = FALSE],
                   cl = factor(wide$class[train]), k = 1))
}
knn_long <- knn_make_spectra()
knn_wide <- knn_to_wide(knn_long)

# image-wise split: spectra 1-2 train, spectrum 3 test
img_train <- knn_wide$spectrum %in% 1:2
img_test  <- knn_wide$spectrum == 3
knn_img_pred <- knn_predict(knn_wide, img_train, img_test)
knn_img_correct <- sum(knn_img_pred == knn_wide$class[img_test])

# animal-wise two-fold group split (same folds as the split plan)
knn_fold <- c(T1 = 2, T2 = 2, T3 = 1, T4 = 1)[knn_wide$id]
knn_ani <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:2, function(f) {
  tr <- knn_fold != f; te <- knn_fold == f
  stopifnot(length(intersect(unique(knn_wide$id[tr]), unique(knn_wide$id[te]))) == 0)
  data.frame(fold = f, id = knn_wide$id[te], class = knn_wide$class[te],
             pred = knn_predict(knn_wide, tr, te))
}))
knn_ani_spectra <- sum(knn_ani$pred == knn_ani$class)
# animal-level vote: the majority class of an animal's three spectra
knn_votes <- aggregate(pred ~ id + class, knn_ani, function(p) names(which.max(table(p))))
knn_ani_animals <- sum(knn_votes$pred == knn_votes$class)

knn_votes
c(image_wise = knn_img_correct, animal_wise_spectra = knn_ani_spectra, animal_wise_animals = knn_ani_animals)

stopifnot(knn_img_correct == 4)                        # recognition of known animals
stopifnot(nrow(knn_ani) == 12, nrow(knn_votes) == 4)   # every animal tested once; denominator 4 animals
stopifnot(knn_ani_spectra == 6, knn_ani_animals == 2, all(knn_ani$pred == "B"))  # reference values for this seed
```

The nearest-neighbour model gets `r knn_img_correct` of 4 spectra right in the image-wise split, because the nearest
spectrum is almost always another spectrum of the same animal. In the two-fold animal-wise split it gets
`r knn_ani_spectra` of 12 spectra and `r knn_ani_animals` of 4 animals right; in this draw it assigned class
`r paste(unique(knn_ani$pred), collapse = " and ")` to every test spectrum, so the hits on the two B animals say nothing
about the class signal. Unlike the hand calculation, these values come from one random draw; the `stopifnot()` line
records them as reference values for seed 4419, not as properties of the method. The independent denominator is four
animals.

```{r}
#| label: fig-b19-spectra
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-cap: "Synthetic reflectance spectra used by the nearest-neighbour variant (reflectance is unitless, 0 to 1; wavelength in nm). Three spectra per animal, n = 4 animals. Each animal has its own level and tilt; class B has a weak dip around 800 nm. Data status: synthetic."
#| fig-alt: "Line chart of reflectance against wavelength from 500 to 940 nanometres. Twelve thin lines in four groups of three, one group per animal, each with its own line type: T1 class A solid, T2 class B dashed, T3 class A long-dashed, T4 class B dash-dotted. All curves rise from about 0.3 below 650 nanometres to between about 0.53 and 0.70 above 750 nanometres. The three lines of each animal lie almost on top of each other, while the four animals are clearly separated by their vertical offset and tilt; the class-B dip near 800 nanometres is small compared with the differences between animals."
knn_long$animal <- paste0(knn_long$id, " (", knn_long$class, ")")
ggplot(knn_long, aes(wavelength_nm, reflectance, group = interaction(id, spectrum),
                     colour = animal, linetype = animal)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.6) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = unname(cdsr_colours[c("blue", "orange", "green", "purple")])) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = cdsr_linetypes) +
  labs(x = "Wavelength (nm)", y = "Reflectance (unitless)", colour = "Animal (class)", linetype = "Animal (class)",
       caption = "Synthetic spectra, seed 4419; 12 spectra from 4 animals.") +
  theme_cdsr()
```

```{r}
#| label: b19-write-data
#| include: false
# teaching file for learners: long format with both fold assignments
knn_long_out <- knn_long[, c("id", "class", "spectrum", "wavelength_nm", "reflectance")]
knn_long_out$reflectance <- round(knn_long_out$reflectance, 5)
knn_long_out$fold_imagewise <- ifelse(knn_long_out$spectrum == 3, "test", "train")
knn_long_out$fold_animalwise <- c(T1 = 2, T2 = 2, T3 = 1, T4 = 1)[knn_long_out$id]
if (dir.exists("../data")) write.csv(knn_long_out, "../data/b19-spectra.csv", row.names = FALSE)
```

### Variation between independent animals

One draw of four animals is a single experiment. To see how much an animal-wise result can vary, the next block draws
200 new synthetic cohorts of four animals with the same generator and repeats both tests. This is the step from "one
number" to "the spread between independent sets of animals".

```{r}
#| label: tbl-b19-repeat
#| tbl-cap: "Accuracy over 200 synthetic cohorts of 4 animals (weak class signal). Image-wise: share of right test spectra (4 per cohort). Animal-wise: share of right animals by majority vote (4 per cohort, two-fold group split). Data status: synthetic."
knn_repeat <- function(class_effect, R = 200, available = NULL) {
  res <- replicate(R, {
    w <- knn_to_wide(knn_make_spectra(class_effect = class_effect))
    tr_img <- w$spectrum %in% 1:2; te_img <- w$spectrum == 3
    img <- mean(knn_predict(w, tr_img, te_img, available) == w$class[te_img])
    fold <- c(T1 = 2, T2 = 2, T3 = 1, T4 = 1)[w$id]
    te <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:2, function(f)
      data.frame(id = w$id[fold == f], class = w$class[fold == f],
                 pred = knn_predict(w, fold != f, fold == f, available))))
    votes <- aggregate(pred ~ id + class, te, function(p) names(which.max(table(p))))
    c(image_wise = img, animal_wise = mean(votes$pred == votes$class))
  })
  t(res)
}
set.seed(4420)
knn_weak <- knn_repeat(class_effect = 0.03)
knn_summary <- data.frame(
  test = c("Image-wise (spectra)", "Animal-wise (animals)"),
  mean = colMeans(knn_weak),
  p05 = apply(knn_weak, 2, quantile, 0.05),
  p95 = apply(knn_weak, 2, quantile, 0.95),
  share_cohorts_at_or_below_half = colMeans(knn_weak <= 0.5)
)
stopifnot(knn_summary$mean[1] > 0.95, knn_summary$mean[2] < 0.7)
knitr::kable(knn_summary, digits = 2, row.names = FALSE,
             col.names = c("Test", "Mean accuracy", "5th percentile", "95th percentile", "Cohorts with accuracy ≤ 0.5"))
```

Over 200 cohorts the image-wise accuracy stays close to 1 (mean `r sprintf("%.2f", knn_summary$mean[1])`), while the
animal-wise accuracy has a mean of `r sprintf("%.2f", knn_summary$mean[2])` and ranges from
`r sprintf("%.2f", knn_summary$p05[2])` to `r sprintf("%.2f", knn_summary$p95[2])` (5th to 95th percentile). In
`r cdsr_percent(knn_summary$share_cohorts_at_or_below_half[2], 0)` of cohorts the animal-wise result is no better than
guessing. The image-wise number is high and stable for the wrong reason.

```{r}
#| label: b19-loao
# leave-one-animal-out on the same kind of cohorts: one fold per animal
set.seed(4422)
knn_loao <- replicate(200, {
  w <- knn_to_wide(knn_make_spectra(class_effect = 0.03))
  mean(sapply(unique(w$id), function(a) {
    p <- knn_predict(w, w$id != a, w$id == a)
    names(which.max(table(p))) == w$class[w$id == a][1]
  }))
})
round(mean(knn_loao), 2)
stopifnot(mean(knn_loao) < 0.5)
```

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Leave-one-animal-out looks like the strictest split, but with four animals and two classes it leaves only one animal of
the held-out class in training. A nearest-neighbour model is then pulled towards the other class. In the 200 synthetic
cohorts above, its mean animal-level accuracy is `r sprintf("%.2f", mean(knn_loao))`, below the 0.5 expected from guessing.
Check the class balance of every training fold in the split plan, and report the per-animal table instead of a single
percentage.
:::

### Deepening: a missing modality as a stress test

Many hyperspectral systems combine a visible-range and a near-infrared sensor. Suppose the target centre has only the
visible sensor (500–660 nm). A stress test asks what happens when the near-infrared part is missing at test time and is
replaced by the training mean, which is a common default in software pipelines. To make the effect visible, the class
signal is set strong (`class_effect = 0.3`), so that the model would work if both sensors were available.

```{r}
#| label: b19-missing-modality
set.seed(4421)
knn_strong <- knn_repeat(class_effect = 0.30)
set.seed(4421)
knn_strong_vis <- knn_repeat(class_effect = 0.30, available = 1:5)  # only 500-660 nm at test time
knn_stress <- rbind(both_sensors = colMeans(knn_strong), visible_only = colMeans(knn_strong_vis))
round(knn_stress, 2)
stopifnot(knn_stress["visible_only", "animal_wise"] < knn_stress["both_sensors", "animal_wise"])
```

With both sensors, the animal-wise accuracy is `r sprintf("%.2f", knn_stress["both_sensors", "animal_wise"])`; with the
near-infrared part missing it drops to `r sprintf("%.2f", knn_stress["visible_only", "animal_wise"])`, because the class
information sits in the part that is missing. The image-wise accuracy falls as well (to
`r sprintf("%.2f", knn_stress["visible_only", "image_wise"])`), since the replaced columns also carried part of each animal's
signature. A stress test of this kind does not replace an external validation at the
new centre. It shows before the study which missing input would make the claim collapse, and it forces the team to
decide in advance what the system should do when an input is absent: stop, warn, or fall back to the standard
assessment.

::: {.callout-note title="Other implementation: Python/scikit-learn"}
**Original implementation.** `GroupKFold` in scikit-learn [@pedregosa2011sklearn], version 1.9.1 of the stable
documentation (accessed 8 November 2026):
[GroupKFold](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.model_selection.GroupKFold.html). With
`groups` set to the animal ID, each animal appears in exactly one test fold; `LeaveOneGroupOut` is the variant with one
animal per fold.

**Concrete advantage.** When an imaging model already lives in a Python pipeline with preprocessing and network
weights, the group split can sit inside the same pipeline object, so every preprocessing step is fitted within the
training fold only.

**What must be identical for a fair comparison.** The input table (`data/b19-spectra.csv`), the group column (`id`),
the fold assignment (import `fold_animalwise` instead of letting each language form its own folds: GroupKFold orders
groups arbitrarily and, since version 1.6, can shuffle them), the metric unit (spectrum or animal), k = 1 with
Euclidean distance, and the tie rule (`class::knn` breaks voting ties at random; with continuous spectra and k = 1, ties
are practically absent). Tolerance: identical predicted classes.

**Shared target value.** Zero shared IDs between training and test in every fold. The order of folds may differ.

**Status.** Conceptual comparison, not executed.
:::

## Counter-check {#sec-b19-countercheck}

Change one assumption: make the class signal ten times stronger (`class_effect` from 0.03 to 0.30). Before you run the
block, predict the direction for each test. Will the image-wise accuracy rise, fall or stay the same? And the
animal-wise accuracy?

```{r}
#| label: b19-countercheck
knn_compare <- rbind(weak_signal = colMeans(knn_weak), strong_signal = colMeans(knn_strong))
round(knn_compare, 2)
stopifnot(knn_compare["strong_signal", "animal_wise"] > knn_compare["weak_signal", "animal_wise"],
          abs(knn_compare["strong_signal", "image_wise"] - knn_compare["weak_signal", "image_wise"]) < 0.05)
```

The image-wise accuracy is practically unchanged (`r sprintf("%.2f", knn_compare["weak_signal", "image_wise"])` and
`r sprintf("%.2f", knn_compare["strong_signal", "image_wise"])`), whereas the animal-wise accuracy rises from
`r sprintf("%.2f", knn_compare["weak_signal", "animal_wise"])` to `r sprintf("%.2f", knn_compare["strong_signal", "animal_wise"])`.
The image-wise test gives the same answer whether or not there is anything to learn about the classes. A test that
cannot tell these two situations apart cannot support a claim about new animals.

## Consequences for patients and operations {#sec-b19-consequences}

**Ethics and the 3Rs.** An uninformative test design wastes animals even when few are used. Reduction under the 3Rs
means minimising the number of animals consistent with the scientific aims, and the NC3Rs stress that this depends on
appropriately designed and analysed studies [@nc3rs3rs]. Measuring many spectra per animal can maximise the
information gathered per animal, which also counts as reduction, but it does not add independent animals; the
experimental unit has to be fixed before the experiment. ARRIVE 2.0 asks authors to state the experimental unit (Essential 10, item 1b) and
to discuss generalisability and translation (item 18) [@percie2020arrive]. For patients, the stake is indirect but
real: a feasibility study justified by a recognition test asks participants for time, measurements and possibly
images, on a premise that was never tested. The fair sentence in an application is the one that names the tested case.

**Regulation.** Not touched while the classifier is a research tool. It becomes relevant once a medical intended
purpose is stated, for example "supports the assessment of tissue perfusion in patients"; then the questions of
@sec-b22 apply, and the evidence must refer to the intended population and setting. A test on known animals is not
clinical evidence for any intended purpose.

**Data protection.** Animal spectra are not personal data. The question changes as soon as patient images are collected
for the next study; the data flow, the legal basis for health data and the deletion point are treated in @sec-b23.

**Security and traceability.** The claim "zero shared IDs" is only as good as the record of which animals were in
which fold. Keep the split plan, the fold file and the model version together and under version control (@sec-b04,
@sec-b24); a model trained later on "all available data" silently changes which animals are new.

## Look up and transfer {#sec-b19-lookup}

- **Reviewer question:** Which unit is new in your test set, how many of these units are there, and is the result
  reported per unit? Please provide the split plan with the number of shared IDs per fold.
- **Self-test:** A team measures six pigs (three of each class) in two laboratories: pigs 1–4 in laboratory 1, pigs
  5–6 in laboratory 2, with 40 spectra per pig. A random 80/20 split of all 240 spectra gives 98% accuracy on 48 test
  spectra. (a) Which claim does this result support? (b) What is the independent denominator for a claim about new pigs?
  (c) Propose a split for a claim about a new laboratory and say what its denominator would be.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
(a) Recognition of further spectra from the six known pigs: with 40 spectra per pig, almost every test spectrum has
spectra of the same pig in training. (b) The number of pigs in the test folds; with a group split over all six pigs, at
most six, and per fold far fewer. Reporting "48 test spectra" overstates the information. (c) Develop in laboratory 1
(pigs 1–4) and test in laboratory 2 (pigs 5–6). The denominator is two pigs, so the only possible results are 0/2, 1/2
and 2/2; check first that laboratory 2 contains both classes. The honest conclusion is that the data cannot support a
claim about new laboratories, and that the next study needs more animals or a second external site, not more spectra
per animal.
:::

- **Annotated sources:**
  - @justice1999generalizability distinguish reproducibility from transportability and give the hierarchy of
    historical, geographic, methodological and spectrum generalisability behind @tbl-b19-levels.
  - @debray2015framework show how to interpret an external validation in light of case-mix differences between
    development and validation samples.
  - @roberts2017crossvalidation explain why random cross-validation underestimates error in clustered data and how to
    block by group, time or space.
  - @kapoor2023leakage survey data leakage across 17 fields and give a taxonomy of leak types.
  - @zech2018pneumonia document that an imaging model could recognise the hospital system of a radiograph, a
    measurement-procedure confounder.
  - @seok2013mouse and @takao2015mouse reach opposite conclusions about mouse–human similarity after trauma and
    inflammation from the same data, which illustrates that "species similarity" depends on analysis choices.
  - @percie2020arrive (ARRIVE 2.0) and @nc3rs3rs (3Rs) frame the experimental unit and the justification of animal
    numbers.
  - @venables2002mass is the reference for the `class` package and `knn()`; @pedregosa2011sklearn for scikit-learn.

The chapter is required reading for W4, where learners split several recordings per animal image-wise and
animal-wise and check the ID intersection in R. In W6 the split plan becomes the template for "the next test on another
cohort, time or species", and in W8 groups defend which new case their model refers to.
